sets.title: Market structure essentials
sets.subject: Economics
sets.description: Original introductory practice: competition, entry barriers and price discrimination.

items.answer: A seller that accepts the market price because it cannot individually influence that price.

items.prompt: What is a barrier to entry?
items.answer: An obstacle that makes it difficult for new firms to enter a market.
Differences, real or perceived, between the products offered by different sellers.
Selling the same product at different prices when the price differences are not explained by cost differences.

items.prompt: Which feature best fits perfect competition?
items.explanation: Perfect competition is characterised by many sellers offering a homogeneous product.

items.prompt: Which is an example of a legal barrier to entry?
items.explanation: A patent grants legal protection that can prevent competitors from using the protected invention.

items.prompt: Why does preventing resale help price discrimination?
choices: It stops lower-price customers reselling to higher-price customers
items.explanation: Resale would undermine separate prices by allowing higher-price customers to buy through the lower-price group.

items.prompt: What does b^2 - 4ac tell you about a quadratic equation?

sets.title: Conditionals: from facts to regrets
sets.subject: English
sets.description: Practise common conditional patterns and choose the form that matches the meaning.

items.prompt: What is the usual zero conditional pattern?
items.answer: If + present simple, present simple. Example: If water reaches its boiling point, it boils.

items.prompt: What is a common first conditional pattern?
items.answer: If + present simple, will + base verb. Example: If I finish early, I will call you.

items.prompt: How do we describe an unreal present situation?
items.answer: If + past simple, would + base verb. Example: If I had more time, I would practise daily.

items.prompt: How do we describe an unreal past situation?
items.answer: If + past perfect, would have + past participle. Example: If I had left earlier, I would have caught the bus.

items.prompt: If she had studied, she ___ the test.
items.explanation: Both the condition and its imagined result refer to the past, so use the third conditional.

items.prompt: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ at home.
items.explanation: This is a possible future condition: present simple in the if-clause, will in the main clause.
